overview.text: American football, also called gridiron football, is a team sport that developed in the United States from rugby and soccer. Rutgers and Princeton played a game commonly identified as the first college football game in 1869; in the 1880s, Yale player Walter Camp helped shape the rules of the developing American game. Teams take turns trying to advance an oval ball by running or passing it forward, while the opposing defense tries to stop them or gain possession. Under NFL rules, an offense has up to four downs to advance 10 yards for a new set of downs. Carrying or catching the ball in the opponent’s end zone scores a six-point touchdown; a kick through the goalposts scores a field goal. Rules can vary by level of play.

key_facts.text: Walter Camp helped codify the game in the 1880s; the Library of Congress credits him with innovations including the 11-player team and quarterback position.
Under NFL rules, an offense earns a new first down by advancing 10 yards within a series of up to four downs.
In the NFL, a touchdown is worth six points and a field goal is worth three; after a touchdown, a team can attempt to score extra points.
Professional football took shape in the 1890s, and team representatives formed a professional league in 1920 that later became the NFL.
The Pro Football Hall of Fame traces the game’s roots to both soccer and rugby, and describes Walter Camp’s rule changes as helping transform rugby into American football.
